659.title: Look to others (Philippians 1:27–2:4)
659.hook: do nothing out of selfish ambition; look to others' interests
659.howItsDone: Some Christian communities take Philippians 2:3–4 as a rule for their life together, and it is often read when churches, families or teams are working through conflict.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man in chains wrote to live is Christ, and to die is gain. Your line was a strait betwixt two. What good did you find inside your constraint? Day six hundred fifty-nine.

Being Romans. That's the phrase the crowd at Philippi uses in the book of Acts, when they drag Paul before the magistrates: these men teach customs, they say, that aren't lawful for us to keep, being Romans. Acts calls the city a colony, a piece of Rome set down in Macedonia. Being Roman mattered there. So when Paul writes to the church in Philippi about how to live, he reaches for a word every one of them knew. The word for being a citizen.

The King James Bible says: "Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ." Conversation, in old English, meant your whole way of life, not just talk. But Paul's Greek word is politeuesthe: live as citizens. Behave as citizens worthy of the good news. Later in the letter he'll say their real citizenship is in heaven. So: you know how to be Roman. Now be citizens of something else, together. Then he asks for something hard, and he asks it warmly. If there's any comfort in Christ, any fellowship of the Spirit, any tenderness, then "Fulfil ye my joy, that ye be likeminded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind." Make my joy complete by getting along. It seems the Philippians had some friction; later he names two women who need to agree. Then the heart of it: "Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves." Vainglory is empty glory: doing things to look good. Lowliness of mind is humility. Some readers point out that in ordinary Greek, lowly could mean servile, beneath you, and Paul turns it into something to aim for. And then: "Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others." Notice that small word: also. Paul doesn't say ignore your own needs. He says don't stop at them. Look at your own things, and also at the things of others. It's a picture of a community where everyone is quietly watching out for someone else, and someone else is watching out for them. And tomorrow, Paul gives the reason: the pattern of Christ himself.
screen: `MAKE MY JOY COMPLETE: BE OF ONE MIND.`
`NO EMPTY GLORY; HUMILITY AS A VIRTUE.`
then, large: `LOOK NOT EVERY MAN ON HIS OWN THINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put someone's interest first. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people you'll be around today: at home, at work, in line, online. Pick one. What do they need today that you could notice? The last good parking spot. The chance to finish their story. Credit for their idea in a meeting. The bigger slice. Choose one specific way to put their interest ahead of yours, without making a show of it. If you pray, you can ask for eyes to see what others need. The bell holds the time.
Vainglory. Paul's word for empty glory, doing things to look good: he asks a proud Roman colony to let humility and others' needs come first instead.
Your line: others first. Today, do the one specific thing you chose, and don't mention that you did it. Day six hundred fifty-nine.

what it means: in a proud Roman colony, live as citizens of something else: no empty glory, and an eye on others' needs as well as your own.

660.title: He emptied himself (Philippians 2:5–11)
660.hook: an early hymn: he took the form of a servant, humbled himself to death
660.carry: all the way down, for others
660.howItsDone: Many churches read Philippians 2:5–11 on Palm Sunday, and in some traditions people bow their heads at the name of Jesus, a custom drawn from this hymn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Roman colony told to live as citizens of something else. Your line was others first. Did anyone notice the thing you did? Day six hundred sixty.

Yesterday Paul asked the Philippians to stop chasing empty glory and to look to each other's needs. Today he gives them the reason, and the rhythm of his writing changes. The sentences start to balance, line against line, like poetry. Many scholars think Paul is quoting a hymn here, something the earliest Christians already sang, within a few decades of the crucifixion. If they're right, these six verses are among the oldest words about Jesus we have. Some think Paul wrote them himself. Either way, the shape is unmistakable: a song that goes all the way down, and then all the way up.
screen: `ALL THE WAY DOWN, ALL THE WAY UP.`

segments.voice: It begins: "Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus." Then the descent. In the King James Bible: "Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men." Made himself of no reputation. The Greek is shorter and sharper: ekenosen, he emptied himself. From that verb comes today's word, kenosis, self-emptying. Notice what the hymn says he didn't do. He didn't treat equality with God as something to grab or cling to. He let go. Then the steps keep going down. A servant. A human being. "he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross." The cross was the death Rome used for slaves and rebels. It doesn't get lower than that. Then the turn. "Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him." All the way up: "That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow," in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. Those lines echo the prophet Isaiah, where God says every knee will bow to him. The hymn hears that promise fulfilled in Jesus. What exactly did he empty himself of? Christians have asked that for centuries. Most churches teach that he didn't stop being God, but set aside the privileges, taking on our limits, our hunger, our death. Some modern theologians have pushed the idea further. All agree on the direction: down, for others. And Paul's point for the Philippians is simple. Yesterday he said, look to others. Here's why: this is the mind of Christ.
screen: `DOWN TO THE DEATH OF THE CROSS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one humble thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of something that needs doing that nobody wants to do, and nobody will thank you for. The bathroom at work. The dishes left in the sink. Taking out a neighbor's trash cans. Listening to someone everyone else avoids. Notice the small voice that says that's not my job. Picture yourself doing it anyway, quietly, the way a servant would. If you pray, you can pray the hymn's first line: let this mind be in me. The bell holds the time.
Kenosis. Greek for self-emptying: the hymn's picture of Christ letting go of his rights and going all the way down, for others.
Your line: all the way down, for others. Today, do the humble thing you pictured, and let nobody know it was you. Day six hundred sixty.

661.title: Shine like stars (Philippians 2:12–18)
661.hook: do everything without grumbling, shining like stars
661.howItsDone: Some Christians take on a fast from complaining for a day or a season, especially in Lent, and some families and youth groups use Philippians 2:14–15 for it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn that went all the way down: kenosis. Your line was all the way down, for others. Did you get the humble thing done without anyone knowing? Day six hundred sixty-one.

Try counting your complaints for one morning. Not the big ones. The small ones. The coffee's cold. The traffic. The meeting that could've been an email. The group chat. The weather, which you can't change and mention anyway. It's easy to lose count before lunch. Grumbling is a kind of background noise of being human. So it's a little startling that, right after the hymn of Christ emptying himself, Paul comes down to earth and says: do everything without grumbling.

First, a famous and much-argued line. In the King James Bible: "work out your own salvation with fear and trembling." And immediately: "For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure." You work it out, because God is working in you. Christians have balanced those two halves differently. Catholic and Orthodox Christians often stress cooperation with grace. Many Protestants stress that the working out flows from a salvation already given. Read either way, the two sentences belong together; one without the other loses Paul's point. Then the practical part: "Do all things without murmurings and disputings." Some readers hear an echo here of Israel in the wilderness, where the King James uses the same word, murmur, for complaints about the food and the water on the long road out of Egypt. If the echo is meant, Paul is reaching for a story his own scriptures already told about how hard trust is on a long road. Then the picture: "That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world." Crooked and perverse echoes the song of Moses in Deuteronomy. And the word for lights is phosteres, the word the old Greek translation of Genesis uses for the lights God set in the sky: sun, moon and stars. So Paul is telling a small church in a Roman town that they can be like stars in a dark sky. Not by being loud, but by not grumbling, by holding forth the word of life. And in the middle, a quiet line about himself: if my life is poured out like an offering, I'm glad. I rejoice with you all.
screen: `WORK IT OUT, FOR GOD IS AT WORK IN YOU.`
then, large: `AMONG WHOM YE SHINE AS LIGHTS IN THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go a day without grumbling. Start now. Settle, and breathe. Notice a complaint already forming about today. Name it, then let it go on the out-breath. Do it again with the next one. Think about the moments today when you're most likely to grumble: the commute, a certain coworker, the dinner dishes. Picture each one, and picture yourself meeting it with quiet instead, or even something kind. If you pray, you can ask for help with the hardest one. The bell holds the time.
Phosteres. Greek for lights, the word Genesis uses for the sun, moon and stars: Paul's picture for a small church, shining without grumbling in a dark sky.
Your line: shine as lights. Today, go the whole day without grumbling, and when you slip, just start again. Day six hundred sixty-one.

662.title: Timothy and Epaphroditus (Philippians 2:19–30)
662.hook: two friends honored: one who cares, one who nearly died serving
662.howItsDone: Many churches remember helpers by name in their prayers and announcements, and some traditions honor Timothy and other companions of Paul with feast days in the church calendar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul asked the Philippians to shine like stars, and your line was shine as lights. Did you manage a whole day without grumbling, or at least half of one? Day six hundred sixty-two.

At the end of a film the credits roll: the grip, the caterer, the person who drove the van. Plenty of people are out the door before they finish. A few lines back, Paul's letter to the Philippians sang of Christ who emptied himself and was lifted up. Now Paul does something that looks almost ordinary. He writes about travel plans. Who's coming to visit, and when, and why. Two names. A man who has served beside him like a son, and a man from Philippi itself who brought a gift and nearly died delivering it. Today the letter stops to roll the credits, and Paul reads them out slowly.

First, Timothy. Paul is in chains, and he hopes to send Timothy to Philippi soon. In the King James Bible he says: "For I have no man likeminded, who will naturally care for your state." Naturally. Not because he's told to. Timothy simply cares. And Paul adds a family picture: "as a son with the father, he hath served with me in the gospel." Acts says Timothy's mother was a Jewish believer and his father Greek, and that Paul took him along on his travels. Then, Epaphroditus. Everything we know about him is in this letter. The church at Philippi sent him to carry their gift to Paul in prison and to stay and help. Somewhere along the way he fell ill. "For indeed he was sick nigh unto death: but God had mercy on him; and not on him only, but on me also, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow." Notice Paul doesn't pretend. He would have grieved. Sorrow on sorrow. And here's a tender detail: Epaphroditus is homesick and heavy-hearted, not about his illness, but because the people back home heard he was ill, and he hates to think of them worrying. So Paul sends him home with an instruction: "Receive him therefore in the Lord with all gladness; and hold such in reputation." Modern versions say honor. Hold people like this in honor. The courier. The helper. The one who almost didn't make it back. In a letter about Christ lowering himself, Paul shows what that looks like in two ordinary lives, and asks the church to lift them up.
screen: then, large: `RECEIVE HIM WITH ALL GLADNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your Epaphroditus. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who helps and is rarely thanked out loud. The person who covers the shift. The neighbor who takes in the packages. The relative who always drives. Picture their face. Remember one specific thing they did, as exactly as you can. Now imagine saying it in front of others, by name, the way Paul did in a letter that would be read aloud to a whole church. What would you say? Keep it short and true. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Epaphroditus. The Philippians' courier who nearly died bringing their gift to Paul in prison, and whom Paul sends home asking the church to hold him in honor.
Your line: hold such in honor. Today, thank one helper where others can hear it: in a meeting, a group chat, at the dinner table. Name what they did. Day six hundred sixty-two.

663.title: Counting it loss (Philippians 3:1–11)
663.hook: everything Paul was proud of, he counts as loss compared with knowing Christ
663.howItsDone: Many Christians read Philippians 3 when thinking about pride and identity, and some churches use verses 7 to 11 in Lent as a reflection on what to set aside.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Timothy and Epaphroditus, the two helpers Paul named, and your line was hold such in honor. Whose name did you say out loud? Day six hundred sixty-three.

A résumé, printed on the good paper, in the right fonts. Born into the right family. Top schools. The best teachers. A record nobody can fault. Then the owner takes a red pen and writes across the whole page, in big letters: loss. Not shredding it. Not lying about it. Just marking it down, as if the numbers had been in the wrong column the whole time. That is close to what Paul does in the third chapter of Philippians. He lays out every credential he ever had, one by one, and then moves the whole list from one side of the ledger to the other.

Here's the list, in the King James Bible: "Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews; as touching the law, a Pharisee." Every item is something to be proud of. He kept the law of his people with great zeal, and says that by its measure of righteousness he was blameless. Notice he is not mocking any of it. These are real goods, an honored family, a faithful upbringing, a serious life. That's what makes the next line land. "But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ." It's bookkeeping language. Gain and loss, profit and debit. Then he goes further: "I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord." All things. And he uses a rough word for them, one that means refuse, the scraps you throw out. Older English Bibles put it bluntly as dung. Why so strong? Because, Paul says, what he wants now is not a record but a person: "That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings." Know, here, is not knowing about. It's the way you know a friend. Christians read this passage in different ways. Some hear a conversion from one way of standing before God to another. Others stress that Paul never stops being a Jew, and that what he counts as loss is his own standing, his pride, not the Torah or his people. Both readings see the turn: the things that once defined him no longer get to.
screen: then, large: `I COUNT ALL THINGS BUT LOSS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one pride. Settle, and breathe. Name something you're proud of that quietly runs your life. A title. A grade. Being the one who's always right, or always busy, or always fine. Don't throw it away. It may be a real good, as Paul's were. Just picture writing it on a card and moving it across the table, out of the center. Notice what's left in the middle when it's gone. Notice if your shoulders change. If you pray, you can hand it to God and leave the card there. The bell holds the time.
Pharisee. Paul's own credential before his bookkeeping turn: a label he moved, with everything else he had, into the loss column, next to knowing Christ.
Your line: all else is loss. Today, when the urge comes to mention your credentials, skip it once, and see whether the conversation is any worse. Day six hundred sixty-three.

664.title: Press on (Philippians 3:12–21)
664.hook: forgetting what lies behind, straining forward
664.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Philippians 3:13–14 at new beginnings, such as a new year, a graduation or a recovery.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul moved his whole résumé into the loss column, and your line was all else is loss. Which pride did you move out of the center? Day six hundred sixty-four.

Watch the last fifty meters of a race. Nobody in the lead looks back. Coaches drill it: the moment you turn your head to see who's behind you, you lose a step. The runners lean forward, chest out, reaching for a line on the ground. Paul reaches for the same picture: a track, a line, a prize. Paul has just told the Philippians that everything behind him is loss. Now he turns around, so to speak, and faces the other way. He reaches for the language of the stadium to say what his life looks like now.

He starts with an admission. Paul, the great apostle, says he hasn't arrived. In the King James Bible: "Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended." Not yet. I haven't got hold of it. Then the famous lines: "this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus." Every phrase is a runner. Forgetting what's behind. Reaching forth, the body leaning out. The mark, the goal at the end of the track. The prize. And the verb for press is worth a second look. In Greek it's a word for chasing, pursuing hard. A few verses earlier, Paul used the very same word about his past: he had been zealous, he said, persecuting the church. Persecuting, chasing. The same energy that once hunted Christians now runs toward Christ. Paul doesn't become a calmer man. He points the same drive in a new direction. What does he mean by forgetting? Not amnesia. He remembers his past well enough to write it down a few verses earlier. He means it no longer steers. Not his old credentials, not his old wrongs. Then he widens the picture, back to the citizen word from a few days ago: "For our conversation is in heaven." You live here, he says, but your city is somewhere else. So you run.
screen: then, large: `I PRESS TOWARD THE MARK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one step forward. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you keep replaying, a failure, an old win, a conversation you can't stop rewriting. Notice how much of your attention it still takes. Now gently turn your head the other way. What is one small thing in front of you, today or this week, that you've been putting off while you looked back? A call. A page. An apology. A first lap. Picture yourself taking the first step toward it, just one. If you pray, you can ask for help to run. The bell holds the time.
Press on. Paul's runner's word: chase hard toward the goal, the same verb he once used for persecuting, now aimed forward.

Your line: forgetting what's behind, reaching forth. Today, do the first lap of the thing you've been postponing, even ten minutes of it, without looking back to grade the last attempt. Day six hundred sixty-four.

665.title: Help these women (Philippians 4:1–3)
665.hook: Euodia and Syntyche, co-workers, are asked to agree
665.howItsDone: Many churches ask a trusted third person, a pastor, elder or friend, to help members reconcile, and some read Philippians 4:2–3 when teaching about peacemaking in the congregation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the runner's verse, and your line was press on. What was the one step you took forward instead of looking back? Day six hundred sixty-five.

Two names, and that's almost all we know. Euodia and Syntyche. Paul's letter is going to be read aloud to the whole church at Philippi, everyone in the room, and in the middle of it he names two women who aren't getting along. We don't know what the quarrel was about. Money, a meeting, a hurt word, a plan for the church. The letter never says, and it's honest to leave it there. What we do know is how Paul handles it. He doesn't take a side. He doesn't send a rebuke. He asks for help.

First he speaks to the whole church with real warmth: they are, in the King James Bible, "my joy and crown." Then: "I beseech Euodias, and beseech Syntyche, that they be of the same mind in the Lord." Notice he says beseech twice, once to each woman. Neither gets named first as the problem. And same mind is a phrase he's used all through this letter: be likeminded, have this mind in you which was also in Christ Jesus. It doesn't mean agreeing on every detail. It means facing the same direction. Then he turns to someone else: "And I intreat thee also, true yokefellow, help those women which laboured with me in the gospel." Who is the yokefellow? Nobody knows. Some think it's a friend Paul doesn't name. Some think Yokefellow, Syzygos in Greek, was the man's actual name. Either way, a third person is asked to step in and help two people find their way back. And look how Paul describes these women. Not as troublemakers. As co-workers who labored with him in the gospel, side by side, along with Clement and the rest, "whose names are in the book of life." Their quarrel doesn't cancel their work. Philippi's church began, Acts says, with women at a place of prayer by a river, and Lydia opening her home. Women were there from the start. This week we've walked through Philippians: look to others, he emptied himself, shine like stars, two helpers honored, counting it loss, press on, and now two co-workers asked to agree.
screen: `CO-WORKERS, NAMES IN THE BOOK OF LIFE.`
then, large: `BE OF THE SAME MIND IN THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be the yokefellow. Settle, and breathe. Think of two people you know who have drifted apart or fallen out. Friends, siblings, coworkers, parents. Don't decide who's right. Paul didn't. Picture each of them, one and then the other, and remember one good thing each has done. Then ask yourself one question: is there a small way you could help, without taking sides? A shared invitation. A kind word about one to the other. Or simply not feeding the quarrel. If you pray, you can hold both of them before God by name. The bell holds the time.
Syzygos. The Greek word for yokefellow, one who pulls in the same yoke, maybe even the man's own name: Paul's friend asked to help Euodia and Syntyche find the same mind again.
Your line: be of one mind. Today, when you hear one person complain about another, say something true and good about the one who isn't there. Day six hundred sixty-five.
